report:
**Conclusion: No — the evidence does not support arthroscopy for knee osteoarthritis.**

Despite the user's expectation, the retrieved evidence consistently shows that arthroscopic surgery is **not** effective for osteoarthritis of the knee.

**Key evidence:**

1. **Landmark RCT (Moseley et al., 2002, NEJM):** A randomized, placebo-controlled trial found no difference between arthroscopic surgery and sham (placebo) surgery in relieving pain or improving function in patients with knee osteoarthritis. ([https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259))

2. **Cochrane systematic review (2022):** Assessed benefits and harms of arthroscopic surgery (debridement, partial meniscectomy, or both) versus placebo or non-surgical treatment for degenerative knee disease. Guidelines strongly advise against its use. ([https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD014328_arthroscopic-surgery-degenerative-knee-disease](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD014328_arthroscopic-surgery-degenerative-knee-disease))

3. **BMJ systematic review and meta-analysis:** Found minimal benefit, with accumulating evidence of minimal benefit in patients with osteoarthritis. ([https://www.bmj.com/content/bmj/350/bmj.h2747.full.pdf](https://www.bmj.com/content/bmj/350/bmj.h2747.full.pdf))

4. **Clinical practice guideline (BMJ 2017):** An expert panel explicitly recommended **against** arthroscopic knee surgery in patients with degenerative knee disease. ([https://www.researchgate.net/publication/323203463_Arthroscopic_surgery_for_degenerative_knee_arthritis_and_meniscal_tears_a_clinical_practice_guideline](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/323203463_Arthroscopic_surgery_for_degenerative_knee_arthritis_and_meniscal_tears_a_clinical_practice_guideline))

Multiple RCTs, a Cochrane review, meta-analyses, and clinical practice guidelines all converge on the same conclusion: arthroscopy offers no meaningful benefit over placebo or conservative treatment for knee osteoarthritis. Some surgeons argue it may help a select group (mild OA with meniscal injury), but this lacks strong Level I evidence.
